A2.text:
Murad is twenty-three. Last month, his girlfriend left him. He was very sad and stayed at home every day.

His grandfather, Hasan, is a fisherman. He has a small boat in the harbour near Shikhov. One Sunday, he said, “Come fishing with me.”

They went out on the Caspian Sea early in the morning. The water was calm. Grandfather Hasan told Murad, “Don't be sad. There are plenty more fish in the sea.”

Murad laughed a little. They waited, but they did not catch anything.

Suddenly, the engine stopped. Grandfather tried to start it, but it did not work. A strong current started to push the boat away from the shore.

“Are we in deep water?” Murad asked. He was scared. He could not swim well, and he was afraid to drown.

“Put on your life jacket,” Grandfather said calmly. “With it, you can float. Don't fight the sea. Go with the flow.”

Grandfather called his friend on the phone. One hour later, his friend came in another boat and pulled them back to the harbour.

On the way back, Murad's line moved. He caught a big fish!

Grandfather smiled. “You see? I told you. Plenty more fish in the sea.”

That evening, Murad felt happy for the first time in a month.

B1.text:
For a month after Aysel ended their relationship, Murad barely left his room. He stopped answering his friends, gave up going to the gym and spent his evenings looking at old photos on his phone.

His grandfather Hasan, who had fished the Caspian for fifty years, finally lost patience. “Tomorrow, five o'clock, the harbour at Shikhov,” he said on the phone. “Bring a jacket.”

The sea was flat and silver when they left. Hasan's little wooden boat moved slowly away from the shore. For an hour, neither of them said much. Then Hasan handed Murad a fishing rod and said, without looking at him, “I know about Aysel. Listen to an old fisherman: there are plenty more fish in the sea.”

“Grandpa, that's the oldest line in the world.”

“It's old because it's true.”

They didn't catch a single thing all morning. Around eleven, the engine coughed twice and died. Hasan tried everything — the fuel, the cable, a few words Murad had never heard him use — but it wouldn't start. Meanwhile, a strong current was carrying them steadily away from land.

Murad's stomach turned. He had never been a strong swimmer, and the shore was getting smaller. “Grandpa, are we in deep water? I mean — are we in trouble?”

“Put on your life jacket,” Hasan said calmly. “It'll keep you floating whatever happens. And stop fighting the sea. When you can't change the current, you go with the flow and wait. People drown because they panic, not because of the water.”

He phoned his old friend Kamil, who had a boat in the same harbour. Kamil arrived an hour later and towed them back to the harbour wall.

They were nearly at the dock when Murad's line suddenly pulled tight. Five minutes later, he lifted a large, shining mullet into the boat.

Hasan laughed until he had to sit down. “What did I tell you? Plenty more fish.”

That night, for the first time in a month, Murad called his friends back.

B2.text:
In the month after Aysel ended things, Murad withdrew from the world almost entirely. He ignored his friends' messages, abandoned the gym and passed his evenings scrolling through photographs he would have been wiser to delete.

His grandfather Hasan, who had fished the Caspian for half a century and regarded self-pity as a waste of daylight, eventually ran out of patience. “Five o'clock tomorrow, Shikhov harbour,” he said. “Bring something warm.”

The sea lay flat and pewter-grey as the little wooden boat slipped away from the shore, oil platforms floating like distant castles on the horizon. For an hour neither man spoke. Then Hasan passed him a rod and remarked, eyes fixed on the water, “I've heard about Aysel. Take it from an old fisherman: there are plenty more fish in the sea.”

“Grandpa, that has to be the oldest line in existence.”

“Things get old by being true.”

They caught nothing all morning. Shortly before eleven, the engine spluttered twice and fell silent. Hasan tried everything in his repertoire — the fuel line, the starter cable, and a vocabulary Murad had never suspected him of possessing — but the motor refused to respond. Meanwhile, a strong current was drawing them steadily away from land. In the Caspian there is almost no tide to bring a boat back; what the current takes, it keeps.

Murad felt his stomach tighten. He had never been a confident swimmer, and the shore was shrinking. “Grandpa — are we in deep water? Figuratively, I mean.”

“Put on the life jacket,” Hasan said, unhurried. “It'll keep you afloat whatever happens. And stop fighting the sea. When the current is stronger than you, you go with the flow and wait for help. People drown because they panic, not because of the water. Your grandmother taught me that on the bank of the Kura, sixty years ago.”

He rang his old friend Kamil, who moored a boat in the same harbour and arrived an hour later, roaring with laughter, to tow them back.

They were almost alongside the harbour wall when Murad's line snapped taut. After five minutes of struggle, he hauled a large, glittering mullet over the side — the only catch of the day.

Hasan laughed until he had to grip the gunwale for support. “Well? What did I say? Plenty more fish.”

That evening, for the first time in a month, Murad answered his friends.

podcast.title: A sea without a tide

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you prefer the sea or a river? Guess: what surprised Sam about the Caspian Sea?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is the sea and rivers. And Leyla, I learned something strange about the Caspian Sea.
What?
There's almost no tide! In England the sea goes out and comes back twice a day.
[laugh] That's because the Caspian is really a giant lake. The water stays where it is.
I went swimming last weekend, at a beach outside Baku. The water was warm, but the current was stronger than I expected.
You have to be careful. Many people swim too far from the shore.
Don't worry, I stayed close. Mostly I just lay on my back and tried to float.
That is what my niece Aysu learned this summer. The first day she was scared, and by the end she was floating like a little boat.
Good for her! When I was a child in Manchester, we didn't have the sea — just a river.
Did you swim in it?
Never! It was too cold. But my grandad and I sat on the river bank every Sunday and tried to catch fish.
Did you catch anything?
One small fish in five years. [chuckle] But I loved those Sundays.
My favourite place is the old harbour in the evening. The boats, the lights, the sound of the water…
Very romantic. My friend Tom needs a place like that. His girlfriend just left him.
Oh, poor Tom. Tell him there are plenty more fish in the sea.
[laugh] That's exactly what I told him! But he's not ready to listen.
Then he should just go with the flow for a while. Stay calm, like the Caspian.
Good advice. I'll send him this episode.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: do you prefer the sea, a river or a lake — and what do you love doing there?
Mine is floating. Just floating. See you next time!
Bye for now!
